text: There is a particular kind of sentence that you meet again and again in official pamphlets, and once you have learned to recognise it you can never again read it without a feeling of mild nausea. It is the sentence that explains, in a tone of weary patience, why some plainly cruel thing had to be done. The villages were not burned; they were pacified. The men were not shot; they were neutralised. The prisoners did not starve; their rations were adjusted to operational realities. What strikes you about this language is not that it lies, exactly, but that it is built to make lying unnecessary. The words have had the blood drained out of them in advance, so that the man who uses them need feel nothing at all. He can sit in a warm office and sign an order that will leave children dead in a ditch, and the paper in front of him will contain no child, no ditch, and no death. I have come to believe that this is the real work such language performs. It does not deceive the public so much as it anaesthetises the official. A man who said plainly what he was doing might hesitate. The whole purpose of the jargon is to see that he never has to.

When I was a boy I was taught that England was a free country, and I believed it, because nobody had yet given me a reason not to. It was only much later, after I had seen how the poor are spoken to in police courts and how the unemployed are made to queue and explain themselves, that I began to understand what the word freedom actually covers and what it quietly leaves out. The freedom was real enough, but it was distributed like everything else, which is to say unevenly and with a careful eye to who you were. A man with money was free to be rude to a constable; a man without it was free to be moved on. I do not say this to be clever. I say it because the gap between the official picture and the thing itself is the most ordinary fact in the world, and yet we spend enormous effort pretending not to notice it. The schoolbook tells you one thing, the street tells you another, and most people learn very early to keep the two accounts in separate drawers. What I want is simply to take both accounts out and lay them side by side on the table, in daylight, and see which one a hungry man would recognise.

I once shared a cell, for a single night, with a man who had stolen a loaf of bread, and I have thought about him a good deal since. He was not a romantic figure. He had a running nose and a way of clearing his throat that got on my nerves within the hour. But what stayed with me was how readily everyone around us, the warders and even the man himself, had agreed that he was a criminal, as though the word settled the matter. Nobody asked why a grown man in a rich country should have to steal bread at all. That question was simply not on the agenda; it had been ruled out long before any of us arrived. This is how a society protects itself from looking at its own arrangements. It invents a category, drops the awkward man into it, and then discusses the category instead of the man. The word criminal did the work that thinking would otherwise have demanded. I do not pretend the fellow was a saint. I only notice that the loaf cost less than the ink spent on his charge sheet, and that nobody in that building seemed troubled by the comparison except, possibly, the thief.

There is a comfortable theory, much beloved of people who have never gone hungry, that the poor are poor chiefly through some defect of character. They drink, they are feckless, they will not save. I have lived among poor people long enough to know that the theory survives only because the comfortable rarely test it against an actual week of poverty. Try, for a single month, living on the wage of a man who cleans drains, paying his rent, eating his food, and see how much of your character is left at the end of it. You will find that the so-called fecklessness is mostly arithmetic. When a man has nothing to save, he does not save; when his only cheap pleasure is a pint, he takes it. None of this requires a moral flaw to explain it. What it requires is a low wage, and the low wage is a decision somebody made, not a law of nature. The great convenience of blaming character is that it asks nothing of the people in charge. They may go on as before, shaking their heads at the improvidence of the poor, while the poor go on doing the only sensible thing a man can do with sixpence, which is to spend it before it is taken from him.

Every age has its sacred words, and you can learn a great deal about an age by noticing which of its words may not be questioned. In ours the word is progress, and it is wheeled out to bless almost anything: a new machine that throws ten men out of work, a road driven through a wood, a form that must now be filled in triplicate where once a handshake served. To stand against any of this is to be called a sentimentalist, an enemy of the future, a man who wants to go back to the candle. I notice that those who use the word loudest are usually those who profit by the change, and that the men thrown out of work are not consulted on whether they feel more progressive than before. I am not against machinery; I am against the trick of language that makes every change automatically a good one merely by attaching a flattering noun to it. A thing should be judged by what it does to actual people in an actual place, not by the warm fog of approval that the word progress spreads over it. Strip the word away and look at the thing itself, and you will often find a perfectly ordinary swindle wearing a halo it has not earned.
